The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence in administrative governance promises
unprecedented efficiency in public service delivery, from automated land-record verification to
predictive resource allocation in healthcare. Proponents argue that algorithmic systems eliminate
human bias, curb bureaucratic delays, and ensure objective adherence to statutory criteria.
However, legal scholars and sociologists caution that algorithms are neither neutral nor infallible;
they inherit the historical inequities embedded within the datasets on which they are trained. When
an automated welfare-eligibility model erroneously flags a marginalised household as ineligible, the
absence of transparent audit trails makes redressal extraordinarily arduous. True administrative
justice requires not merely computational speed, but explainability, human oversight, and
institutional accountability. Without robust regulatory guardrails, technological determinism risks
replacing accountable human discretion with an opaque "black box" bureaucracy.

Comprehension Passage – II (Questions 46 – 50): Read the following passage carefully and
answer the questions that follow.
Mangrove forests, thriving at the dynamic interface between terrestrial and marine ecosystems
along tropical coastlines, serve as nature's most formidable bioshields. Their intricate web of stilt
roots dissipates wave energy, attenuates storm surges, and stabilises coastal sediments against
relentless tidal erosion. Beyond coastal defence, mangroves sequester carbon at rates up to four
times higher per hectare than mature tropical rainforests, locking vast quantities of "blue carbon"
within waterlogged, anaerobic soils for millennia. Yet, aquaculture expansion, coastal urbanisation,
and altered riverine freshwater flows have severely degraded these vital habitats. Restoring
mangroves demands more than indiscriminate sapling plantation; it requires restoring natural
hydrological regimes so that native species can regenerate organically.
